mcq.explanation: Services provide stable access to a set of Pods: Pods come and go with changing IPs, while a Service gives a fixed virtual IP and DNS name and load-balances across whichever matching Pods are ready.
mcq.distractors: Compiling code, building images and storing Git history happen outside Kubernetes.

mcq.explanation: ClusterIP is the default type and is reachable only within the cluster through its virtual IP and DNS name.
mcq.distractors: NodePort and LoadBalancer add external access; ExternalName just returns a DNS CNAME to an outside name and has no cluster IP.

mcq.explanation: NodePort exposes the Service on the same port (default range 30000-32767) on every node, so `<node-IP>:<nodePort>` reaches it from outside.
mcq.distractors: ExternalName is a DNS alias, a headless Service has no virtual IP, and ClusterIP is internal only. (LoadBalancer Services usually allocate a NodePort too, but NodePort is the type defined by that behaviour.)

mcq.explanation: LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider's controller to provision an external load balancer (e.g. an AWS NLB) that forwards to the Service; on bare metal you need something like MetalLB.
mcq.distractors: ClusterIP is internal, ExternalName is just a DNS alias, and headless Services skip load balancing entirely.

mcq.explanation: A Service finds its backend Pods with a label selector: Pods whose labels match `spec.selector` and are ready become its endpoints (tracked in EndpointSlices).
mcq.distractors: Node hostnames, Git branches and image digests play no part in Service routing.

mcq.explanation: `targetPort` is the port on backend Pods (the container port) that traffic is forwarded to; `port` is the port the Service itself listens on. They may differ, e.g. port 80 -> targetPort 8080, and targetPort can be a named container port.
mcq.distractors: Node SSH ports, Git remotes and the API server port are unrelated.

mcq.explanation: kube-proxy implements Service traffic routing rules on each node, programming iptables, IPVS or nftables so traffic to a Service IP is load-balanced to endpoint Pods. (Some CNIs such as Cilium can replace it with eBPF.)
mcq.distractors: Scheduling is the scheduler's job, secrets are stored by the API server in etcd, and kube-proxy builds nothing.

mcq.explanation: `<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local` is the fully qualified Service DNS name, so `db.prod.svc.cluster.local` reaches Service `db` in namespace `prod` from anywhere in the cluster (assuming the default `cluster.local` domain).
mcq.distractors: The other forms are made up and do not match CoreDNS's Kubernetes naming scheme.

mcq.explanation: A headless Service sets `clusterIP: None`: no virtual IP is allocated and DNS returns the individual Pod IPs, which StatefulSets use for stable per-Pod names.
mcq.distractors: replicas belongs to workloads, NodePort is a different Service type, and hostNetwork is a Pod setting.

mcq.explanation: `kubectl get svc` (short for services) lists Services with their type, cluster IP, external IP and ports.
mcq.distractors: build/init are not kubectl verbs and `images` is not a Kubernetes resource.

checks.label: Creates a Service (kind: Service / kubectl expose)
Uses type ClusterIP (explicit or the default)

labs.modelAnswer:
# deploy.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: web
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: web
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:1.27
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80

# Commands
kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
kubectl get pods -l app=web -o wide          # note the 3 Pod IPs
kubectl get svc web                          # TYPE ClusterIP, CLUSTER-IP assigned
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web   # the same 3 Pod IPs on port 80
kubectl describe svc web                     # Selector app=web, Endpoints list
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://web
labs.explanation: Tests that the Service selector matches the Pod template labels so the Service gets endpoints. Verify the EndpointSlice (or `kubectl describe svc`) lists one address per ready Pod, matching `kubectl get pods -o wide`, and that a request from inside the cluster to the Service name succeeds. `kubectl get endpoints` still works but is deprecated in favour of EndpointSlices since Kubernetes 1.33.

checks.label: Checks the assigned port (kubectl get svc)
Accesses the app via the node port (curl / browser)

labs.modelAnswer:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2

# web-nodeport.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-nodeport
spec:
  type: NodePort
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 80
      nodePort: 30080      # optional; must be in 30000-32767

kubectl apply -f web-nodeport.yaml
kubectl get svc web-nodeport               # PORT(S) 80:30080/TCP
kubectl get nodes -o wide                  # INTERNAL-IP of any node
curl http://<node-ip>:30080                # nginx welcome page
# minikube: minikube service web-nodeport --url   (or curl http://$(minikube ip):30080)
# kind: the node is a Docker container, so map the port with extraPortMappings
#       or use: kubectl port-forward svc/web-nodeport 8080:80
labs.explanation: Tests exposing a workload outside the cluster with NodePort. Check that the Service shows `80:3xxxx/TCP`, that the request goes to a node IP (not the ClusterIP or Pod IP) on the node port, and that it returns the app. On local clusters (minikube, kind, Docker Desktop) the node IP may not be reachable from the host, so the helper command or port mapping used should be explained.

checks.label: Sends traffic to the Service port (curl / wget / port-forward)

labs.modelAnswer:
kubectl create deployment web --image=nginx:1.27 --replicas=2   # nginx listens on 80

# web-svc.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: web-svc
spec:
  selector:
    app: web
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 8080        # what clients connect to
      targetPort: 80    # the container port that receives traffic

kubectl apply -f web-svc.yaml
kubectl describe svc web-svc        # Port: http 8080/TCP, TargetPort: 80/TCP, Endpoints: <pod-ip>:80,...
kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=web-svc   # PORTS 80
kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- http://web-svc:8080   # works
kubectl run tmp2 --rm -it --image=busybox:1.36 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://web-svc:80 # times out: Service is not listening on 80
labs.explanation: Tests the difference between `port` (what the Service listens on) and `targetPort` (the container port). Verify that clients use the Service port (8080) and that endpoints show the Pod IPs on the target port (80). A wrong targetPort is a classic cause of connection refused even though the Service has endpoints.
